# Alma — Lead Management

A public lead-capture form and an internal, auth-guarded dashboard for managing
the leads it produces.

- **Public** — a prospect submits their name, email and resume. No account needed.
- **Emails** — on submission, a confirmation goes to the prospect and a notification to an attorney.
- **Internal** — attorneys sign in, browse and search leads, download resumes, and move a lead from `PENDING` to `REACHED_OUT`.

**Stack:** Next.js 15 (App Router) · FastAPI · PostgreSQL · MinIO (S3) · MailHog (SMTP)

---

## Quick start

Requires Docker.

```bash
make up     # build and start everything
make seed   # create the attorney login
```

| Surface | URL | Credentials |
|---|---|---|
| Public form | http://localhost:3000/apply | — |
| Internal dashboard | http://localhost:3000/admin/leads | `attorney@example.com` / `changeme123` |
| API docs (Swagger) | http://localhost:8000/docs | — |
| MailHog inbox | http://localhost:8025 | — |
| MinIO console | http://localhost:9001 | `minioadmin` / `minioadmin` |

Submit the form at `/apply`, then open **MailHog** to read both emails and
**`/admin/leads`** to work the lead.

`make help` lists every target.

> **Port note:** Postgres is published on host port **5433**, not 5432, because
> 5432 is commonly already taken. Change `POSTGRES_HOST_PORT` in `.env` if
> needed — it does not affect container-to-container traffic.

---

## Layout

```
backend/                          FastAPI service
  app/
    api/v1/routes/                HTTP layer only
    services/                     business rules (state machine, email orchestration)
    repositories/                 all database queries
    models/                       SQLAlchemy ORM
    schemas/                      Pydantic request/response contracts
    integrations/
      storage/                    StorageBackend port: s3 | local
      email/                      EmailBackend port: smtp | console
    validators/upload.py          magic-byte resume validation
    templates/email/              Jinja2 HTML + text emails
    core/                         config, security, logging, errors, rate limiting
  alembic/versions/               migrations
  tests/                          68 tests against real Postgres

frontend/                         Next.js app
  src/
    app/apply/                    public form
    app/admin/                    auth-guarded dashboard
    app/api/                      route handlers (cookie exchange, resume proxy)
    components/ui/                Button, Field, Badge, Alert primitives
    lib/                          typed API client, session, formatting
    middleware.ts                 /admin route guard

docs/
  system-design.md                architecture and the decisions behind it
  api.md                          endpoint reference
```

Layering is strict and one-directional:
`routes → services → repositories → models`. Routes never touch the database;
repositories never contain business rules.

---

## Common tasks

```bash
make test         # backend test suite
make lint         # ruff + eslint
make logs         # tail all services
make psql         # open a database shell
make migrate      # apply migrations
make clean        # tear down and delete all data
```

Frontend checks:

```bash
docker compose exec frontend npm run typecheck
docker compose exec frontend npm run build
```

Managing attorney accounts:

```bash
docker compose exec backend python -m app.cli create-user --email a@b.com --name "A B"
docker compose exec backend python -m app.cli deactivate-user --email a@b.com
```

Deactivating preserves the account's audit trail; deleting it would not. See
[docs/system-design.md](docs/system-design.md#why-is_active-instead-of-deleting-attorneys).

---

## Configuration

Everything is environment-driven. `make up` copies `.env.example` to `.env` on
first run; the defaults work out of the box.

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | Postgres connection string |
| `JWT_SECRET` | Token signing key — **replace before deploying** |
| `STORAGE_BACKEND` | `s3` (MinIO/AWS) or `local` (disk) |
| `EMAIL_BACKEND` | `smtp` (MailHog/any relay) or `console` (logs only) |
| `ATTORNEY_NOTIFICATION_EMAIL` | Who receives new-lead notifications |
| `MAX_RESUME_SIZE_BYTES` | Upload cap, default 5 MB |
| `SEED_ADMIN_*` | Account created by `make seed` |

Swapping to a real provider is a config change, not a code change: point
`SMTP_HOST` at SendGrid/SES, or set `STORAGE_BACKEND=s3` with real AWS
credentials.

---

## Notes on the implementation

A few decisions that aren't obvious from the code alone — all covered in depth
in [docs/system-design.md](docs/system-design.md):

**Resume uploads are validated by their bytes, not their name.** The `accept`
attribute and the declared `Content-Type` are both client-controlled, so the
authoritative check sniffs magic bytes: `%PDF-` for PDF, and for DOCX a zip
whose central directory actually contains `word/`. An executable renamed to
`.pdf` is rejected with a 415.

**Emails use a transactional outbox.** Both messages are written as rows in the
same database transaction as the lead itself, so a lead can never exist without
a durable record of the emails owed on it. Delivery is attempted afterwards,
off the request path — a mail outage cannot lose a notification or show the
prospect an error. Delivery status is visible per-lead in the dashboard.

**The state machine lives in one table.** `ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS` in
`services/state_machine.py` is the single source of truth; illegal moves return
409. `REACHED_OUT → PENDING` is deliberately absent.

**Auth is httpOnly-cookie based.** FastAPI issues the JWT; a Next.js route
handler puts it in an httpOnly cookie so no script can read it. `middleware.ts`
guards `/admin` for UX, but real enforcement is FastAPI re-validating the token
*and re-checking the account* on every request — so deactivating an attorney
takes effect immediately rather than at token expiry.

### Known limitations

- **Email retry is not implemented.** A failed delivery is recorded as `FAILED` and surfaced in the UI, but nothing retries it. The schema (`attempts`, `next_attempt_at`) already supports it, so the worker is a pure addition.
- **Rate limiting is in-process.** Correct for one instance; a multi-replica deployment needs Redis or edge limiting.
- **Logout is client-side.** JWTs are stateless, so the token stays valid until it expires. Immediate revocation needs a blocklist or short-lived tokens plus refresh.

`routes → services → repositories → models`. Routes never touch the database;
repositories never contain business rules.

---

## Common tasks

```bash
make test         # backend test suite
make lint         # ruff + eslint
make logs         # tail all services
make psql         # open a database shell
make migrate      # apply migrations
make clean        # tear down and delete all data
```

Frontend checks:

```bash
docker compose exec frontend npm run typecheck
docker compose exec frontend npm run build
```

Managing attorney accounts:

```bash
docker compose exec backend python -m app.cli create-user --email a@b.com --name "A B"
docker compose exec backend python -m app.cli deactivate-user --email a@b.com
```

Deactivating preserves the account's audit trail; deleting it would not. See
[docs/system-design.md](docs/system-design.md#why-is_active-instead-of-deleting-attorneys).

---

## Configuration

Everything is environment-driven. `make up` copies `.env.example` to `.env` on
first run; the defaults work out of the box.

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | Postgres connection string |
| `JWT_SECRET` | Token signing key — **replace before deploying** |
| `STORAGE_BACKEND` | `s3` (MinIO/AWS) or `local` (disk) |
| `EMAIL_BACKEND` | `smtp` (MailHog/any relay) or `console` (logs only) |
| `ATTORNEY_NOTIFICATION_EMAIL` | Who receives new-lead notifications |
| `MAX_RESUME_SIZE_BYTES` | Upload cap, default 5 MB |
| `SEED_ADMIN_*` | Account created by `make seed` |

`SMTP_HOST` at SendGrid/SES, or set `STORAGE_BACKEND=s3` with real AWS
credentials.

---

## Notes on the implementation

A few decisions that aren't obvious from the code alone — all covered in depth
in [docs/system-design.md](docs/system-design.md):

**Resume uploads are validated by their bytes, not their name.** The `accept`
attribute and the declared `Content-Type` are both client-controlled, so the
authoritative check sniffs magic bytes: `%PDF-` for PDF, and for DOCX a zip
whose central directory actually contains `word/`. An executable renamed to
`.pdf` is rejected with a 415.

**Emails use a transactional outbox.** Both messages are written as rows in the
same database transaction as the lead itself, so a lead can never exist without
a durable record of the emails owed on it. Delivery is attempted afterwards,
off the request path — a mail outage cannot lose a notification or show the
prospect an error. Delivery status is visible per-lead in the dashboard.

**The state machine lives in one table.** `ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS` in
`services/state_machine.py` is the single source of truth; illegal moves return
409. `REACHED_OUT → PENDING` is deliberately absent.

**Auth is httpOnly-cookie based.** FastAPI issues the JWT; a Next.js route
handler puts it in an httpOnly cookie so no script can read it. `middleware.ts`
guards `/admin` for UX, but real enforcement is FastAPI re-validating the token
*and re-checking the account* on every request — so deactivating an attorney
takes effect immediately rather than at token expiry.

### Known limitations

- **Email retry is not implemented.** A failed delivery is recorded as `FAILED` and surfaced in the UI, but nothing retries it. The schema (`attempts`, `next_attempt_at`) already supports it, so the worker is a pure addition.
- **Rate limiting is in-process.** Correct for one instance; a multi-replica deployment needs Redis or edge limiting.
- **Logout is client-side.** JWTs are stateless, so the token stays valid until it expires. Immediate revocation needs a blocklist or short-lived tokens plus refresh.

# System design

## 1. Requirements

**Functional**

1. A publicly reachable form captures first name, last name, email and a resume/CV.
2. On submission, email both the prospect and an attorney.
3. An authenticated internal UI lists leads with everything the prospect submitted.
4. A lead starts `PENDING` and moves to `REACHED_OUT` when an attorney marks it manually.

**Non-functional targets**

- A prospect never loses a submission because a downstream dependency is unhealthy.
- Every state change is attributable to a person and a time.
- Storage and email are swappable without touching business logic.
- The public endpoint is exposed to the internet and must be defensible.

---

## 2. Architecture

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
   prospect ───────▶│  Next.js  /apply                │
   (no auth)        │  client-side POST ─────────────┐│
                    └─────────────────────────────────┘│
                                                       │
   attorney ───────▶┌─────────────────────────────────┐│
   (httpOnly        │  Next.js  /admin/*              ││
    cookie)         │  server components + actions    ││
                    │  middleware.ts route guard      ││
                    └──────────────┬──────────────────┘│
                                   │ Bearer JWT        │ multipart
                                   ▼                   ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │  FastAPI                                │
                    │                                         │
                    │  routes      HTTP concerns only         │
                    │     ↓                                   │
                    │  services    state machine, orchestration│
                    │     ↓                                   │
                    │  repositories  all SQL                  │
                    │     ↓                                   │
                    │  models      SQLAlchemy ORM             │
                    │                                         │
                    │  ports:  StorageBackend  EmailBackend   │
                    └───┬──────────────┬─────────────┬────────┘
                        │              │             │
                  ┌─────▼────┐   ┌─────▼─────┐  ┌────▼──────┐
                  │ Postgres │   │ S3/MinIO  │  │ SMTP relay│
                  └──────────┘   └───────────┘  └───────────┘
```

Dependencies point one way. A route never issues SQL; a repository never
decides whether a transition is legal. The two external systems the app does
not own — object storage and email — sit behind ports, so tests run against
in-memory fakes with no network, and production swaps adapters via config.

---

## 3. Data model

```
users                          leads
─────                          ─────
id            uuid PK          id                  uuid PK
email         unique           first_name, last_name
hashed_password                email
full_name                      resume_key          ← opaque, server-generated
is_active     bool             resume_filename     ← prospect's original name
created_at                     resume_content_type, resume_size_bytes
                               state               enum(PENDING, REACHED_OUT)
                               reached_out_at
                               reached_out_by_id   → users.id  (SET NULL)
                               created_at, updated_at

lead_state_events              email_deliveries
─────────────────              ────────────────
id            uuid PK          id                uuid PK
lead_id       → leads (CASCADE) lead_id          → leads (CASCADE)
from_state    nullable         kind              enum(PROSPECT_…, ATTORNEY_…)
to_state                       to_address, subject
actor_id      → users (SET NULL) status          enum(PENDING, SENT, FAILED)
created_at                     attempts, provider_message_id
                               last_error, sent_at
                               next_attempt_at   ← reserved for retry
```

**Indexes.** `(state, created_at)` on `leads` serves the dashboard's default
query — filter by state, newest first — from one index. `email` is indexed for
search. `email_deliveries.status` supports "what is still owed?".

**`lead_state_events` is append-only.** Without it, `state` is a single mutable
cell and the answer to "who marked this, and when?" is lost on the next write.
With it, every transition is a row: the initial `NULL → PENDING` is attributed
to the prospect (`actor_id` is null), and each later move to an attorney.

---

## 4. Key decisions

### 4.1 The transactional outbox

The obvious implementation sends email inline:

```python
lead = create_lead(...)          # committed
send_email(prospect)             # ← blocks the response
send_email(attorney)
return 201
```

This has two failure modes, and the second is the dangerous one:

1. The prospect waits on your mail provider's handshake — seconds of spinner on a public form.
2. If SMTP is down, you must choose: return **500** (but the lead *is already saved*, so they resubmit and you get duplicates), or swallow the error and return **201** (the attorney never learns the lead exists, and nothing anywhere records that). The second choice fails **silently**.

Moving the send to a background task fixes the latency but not the loss: the
intent to send lives only in process memory, so a crash or a failed send
evaporates with no record that anything was owed.

**What we do instead:**

```
BEGIN
  INSERT lead
  INSERT email_deliveries (PROSPECT_CONFIRMATION, PENDING)
  INSERT email_deliveries (ATTORNEY_NOTIFICATION, PENDING)
COMMIT                    ← atomic: all three, or none
   │
   └─▶ 201 returned here. Never blocked on SMTP.
   │
   └─▶ background task, own session:
         success → SENT,   sent_at, provider_message_id
         failure → FAILED, attempts += 1, last_error
```

The guarantee comes from the `COMMIT`. Because the delivery rows are written in
the *same transaction* as the lead, there is no window in which a lead exists
without a durable record of the emails owed on it — that is an atomicity
property of Postgres, not a convention we have to remember. And because the
response is returned immediately after commit, the prospect's experience is
fully decoupled from the mail provider's uptime.

The payoff beyond correctness is **observability**: because every attempt is a
row, "which leads never got their attorney notification?" is a `WHERE` clause,
and delivery status renders directly on the lead detail page. Without it, that
question is unanswerable after the fact.

> **Verified in practice.** During development the dispatch task raced the
> commit and found no lead. The outbox did exactly its job: the lead and both
> delivery rows had committed atomically, nothing was lost, and the two emails
> sat visible as `PENDING`. The fix was to commit before scheduling dispatch.
> Covered by `test_email_failure_does_not_fail_the_submission`.

**Scope limit — retry is not implemented.** A `FAILED` row stays failed. This
was a deliberate call to keep v1 small; `attempts` and `next_attempt_at` are
already in the schema so the worker is a pure addition. See §7.

### 4.2 Resume validation by content, not filename

Three layers, only the third of which is trustworthy:

| Layer | Value |
|---|---|
| `accept` attribute | UX hint. Trivially bypassed. |
| Extension + declared `Content-Type` | Cheap first filter. Client-controlled. |
| **Magic-byte sniffing of the received bytes** | **The check that counts.** |

PDF must begin `%PDF-`. DOCX must begin `PK\x03\x04` *and* be a zip whose
central directory contains `[Content_Types].xml` and a `word/` entry — a plain
zip renamed `.docx` is rejected. Only the directory is read, never extracted,
so a zip bomb has nothing to expand into.

Legacy `.doc` is not supported: it is an OLE2 compound binary that costs real
complexity to validate and is effectively extinct.

Size is enforced by a running byte counter while streaming, not by trusting
`Content-Length`, and the upload is buffered in a `SpooledTemporaryFile` that
rolls to disk past 1 MB so a large upload cannot pin memory.

**Storage keys are generated, never derived from user input:**
`leads/{lead_id}/resume-{random}.pdf`. The prospect's filename is attacker
controlled — using it as a key invites path traversal and cross-lead
overwrites. It is stored in a column purely to set `Content-Disposition` on
download. (`test_resume_is_stored_under_a_generated_key` submits
`../../etc/passwd.pdf` and asserts the key is unaffected.)

**Ordering.** The file is uploaded to object storage *before* the transaction
commits. A crash in between leaves an orphaned object — harmless and cheap to
sweep. The reverse order would leave a lead row pointing at a resume that does
not exist, which is user-visible corruption.

### 4.3 Why `is_active` instead of deleting attorneys

`leads.reached_out_by_id` and `lead_state_events.actor_id` are foreign keys
into `users`. When an attorney leaves:

- **Delete the row** → the FK nulls out and you lose the answer to "who marked this lead as reached out". The audit trail develops holes exactly where accountability matters.
- **Set `is_active = false`** → history stays intact, and one check in the login path stops them signing in.

It exists so that *revoking access* and *destroying history* are not the same
operation.

Critically, `is_active` is re-checked **on every request**, not just at login.
A JWT stays cryptographically valid until it expires, so trusting the token's
claims would leave a deactivated attorney with up to an hour of access.
`test_deactivation_invalidates_an_existing_token` pins this behaviour.

### 4.4 The state machine

```python
ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS = {
    PENDING:     {REACHED_OUT},
    REACHED_OUT: frozenset(),      # terminal
}
```

One table, one place to change. Illegal moves return **409** with the current
state and the legal targets, so the client can render something useful rather
than "something went wrong".

`REACHED_OUT → PENDING` is absent by design: "we un-contacted them" is not a
real event, and allowing it would make the audit trail misleading.

### 4.5 Authentication

FastAPI is the sole auth authority. The browser never holds a readable token:

```
login form ──▶ Next route handler ──▶ FastAPI /auth/login
                     │                      │
                     │◀───── JWT ───────────┘
                     ▼
              Set-Cookie: httpOnly, sameSite=lax, secure in prod
                     │
server components ───┴──▶ read cookie ──▶ Authorization: Bearer ──▶ FastAPI
```

- **httpOnly** — an XSS bug cannot exfiltrate the session.
- **sameSite=lax** — blocks CSRF on cross-site POSTs while surviving normal navigation.
- **`middleware.ts`** — a cheap cookie-presence check so a signed-out visitor never sees an admin shell. It is *not* security: a forged cookie sails past it into a 401 from FastAPI, which verifies the signature and re-checks the account.

Login uses a plain `str` for email rather than `EmailStr`: it is matched against
an existing account, not accepted as new data, and strict validation there would
lock out accounts on internal domains without making anything safer. Response
schemas likewise use `str` — re-validating stored data on the way out turns a
data quirk into a 500.

### 4.6 Resume download

Prefer a **presigned URL**: the API returns a 302 and the bytes flow straight
from object storage to the browser, never through the application. The Next.js
route handler at `/api/leads/[id]/resume` exists because a plain `<a href>`
carries no `Authorization` header — it attaches the token server-side and
forwards the redirect.

The local-disk adapter cannot presign, so it streams through the API instead.
Both paths are exercised: production uses the redirect, tests use the stream.

---

## 5. Request flows

**Public submission**

```
POST /api/v1/leads (multipart)
  → rate limit (per IP, sliding window)
  → validate fields                    422 on bad input
  → sniff magic bytes, enforce cap     415 / 413
  → upload to object storage           500 only if storage itself fails
  → BEGIN … INSERT lead + 2 outbox rows … COMMIT
  → 201  ◀── prospect is done here
  → background: attempt both sends, record outcome
```

**Marking a lead reached out**

```
PATCH /api/v1/leads/{id}  {"state": "REACHED_OUT"}
  → verify JWT, re-check is_active     401
  → load lead                          404
  → assert_can_transition()            409
  → set state, reached_out_at, reached_out_by
  → append lead_state_event
  → return the lead with its full audit trail
```

---

## 6. Failure modes

| Failure | Behaviour | Prospect sees |
|---|---|---|
| SMTP unreachable | Rows marked `FAILED` with the error; visible in the UI | `201` — nothing wrong |
| Object storage down | Upload fails before commit; no partial lead | `500`, safe to retry |
| Database down | Nothing commits; no orphaned storage object beyond a stray file | `500`, safe to retry |
| Process dies mid-dispatch | Rows stay `PENDING`; queryable and visible | `201` — already delivered |
| Malicious upload | Rejected at the byte level | `415` |
| Form spam | Sliding-window limiter | `429` with `retry_after_seconds` |
| Token expires mid-session | `apiFetch` catches the 401 | Redirected to login with a notice |

---

## 7. What I'd do next

Ordered by what I'd reach for first in production.

1. **Email retry worker.** The schema is ready. A loop selecting `status != 'SENT' AND attempts < 5 AND next_attempt_at <= now()` with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (so replicas don't double-send) and exponential backoff. Delivery becomes at-least-once; a duplicate confirmation beats a silent loss.
2. **Distributed rate limiting.** The current limiter is in-process — correct for one instance, useless across replicas and reset on deploy. Move to Redis or the edge.
3. **Virus scanning.** Magic-byte validation proves a file is a well-formed PDF, not that it is safe. A real deployment should scan resumes (ClamAV or a managed scanner) before an attorney downloads one.
4. **Token revocation.** Logout currently just drops the cookie; the JWT stays valid until expiry. Short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token, or a revocation list.
5. **Observability.** Logs are already structured JSON with request ids. Next: metrics on submission rate, delivery failure rate and transition latency, plus an alert on `FAILED` deliveries.
6. **Richer lead pipeline.** More states (`IN_REVIEW`, `QUALIFIED`, `REJECTED`), assignment to a specific attorney, and internal notes. The state machine and audit table were built to absorb this without restructuring.
7. **Idempotency on submission.** An `Idempotency-Key` header would let a client retry a timed-out POST without creating a duplicate lead.

---

## 8. Testing

68 tests. Integration tests run against **real Postgres**, not SQLite, so the
enum types, server defaults and cascade behaviour under test are the ones that
ship. Storage and email use in-memory fakes — the suite is fast, deterministic
and offline.

| File | Covers |
|---|---|
| `test_state_machine.py` | Legal and illegal transitions, 409 payloads |
| `test_upload_validation.py` | Spoofed extensions, zip-not-docx, size cap, content-beats-name |
| `test_rate_limit.py` | Budget, per-client isolation, window expiry |
| `test_auth.py` | Login, case-insensitivity, enumeration resistance, mid-session deactivation |
| `test_leads_public.py` | Intake, outbox atomicity, mail-failure isolation, validation |
| `test_leads_internal.py` | Access control, pagination, search, transitions, audit trail, download |

The tests worth reading first are
`test_email_failure_does_not_fail_the_submission` (the outbox guarantee),
`test_deactivation_invalidates_an_existing_token` (why `is_active` is checked
per-request), and `test_resume_is_stored_under_a_generated_key` (path traversal).

claims would leave a deactivated attorney with up to an hour of access.
`test_deactivation_invalidates_an_existing_token` pins this behaviour.

### 4.4 The state machine

```python
ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS = {
    PENDING:     {REACHED_OUT},
    REACHED_OUT: frozenset(),      # terminal
}
```

One table, one place to change. Illegal moves return **409** with the current
state and the legal targets, so the client can render something useful rather
than "something went wrong".

`REACHED_OUT → PENDING` is absent by design: "we un-contacted them" is not a
real event, and allowing it would make the audit trail misleading.

### 4.5 Authentication

FastAPI is the sole auth authority. The browser never holds a readable token:

```
login form ──▶ Next route handler ──▶ FastAPI /auth/login
                     │                      │
                     │◀───── JWT ───────────┘
                     ▼
              Set-Cookie: httpOnly, sameSite=lax, secure in prod
                     │
server components ───┴──▶ read cookie ──▶ Authorization: Bearer ──▶ FastAPI
```

- **httpOnly** — an XSS bug cannot exfiltrate the session.
- **sameSite=lax** — blocks CSRF on cross-site POSTs while surviving normal navigation.
- **`middleware.ts`** — a cheap cookie-presence check so a signed-out visitor never sees an admin shell. It is *not* security: a forged cookie sails past it into a 401 from FastAPI, which verifies the signature and re-checks the account.

Login uses a plain `str` for email rather than `EmailStr`: it is matched against
an existing account, not accepted as new data, and strict validation there would
lock out accounts on internal domains without making anything safer. Response
schemas likewise use `str` — re-validating stored data on the way out turns a
data quirk into a 500.

### 4.6 Resume download

Prefer a **presigned URL**: the API returns a 302 and the bytes flow straight
from object storage to the browser, never through the application. The Next.js
route handler at `/api/leads/[id]/resume` exists because a plain `<a href>`
carries no `Authorization` header — it attaches the token server-side and
forwards the redirect.

The local-disk adapter cannot presign, so it streams through the API instead.
Both paths are exercised: production uses the redirect, tests use the stream.

---

## 5. Request flows

**Public submission**

```
POST /api/v1/leads (multipart)
  → rate limit (per IP, sliding window)
  → validate fields                    422 on bad input
  → sniff magic bytes, enforce cap     415 / 413
  → upload to object storage           500 only if storage itself fails
  → BEGIN … INSERT lead + 2 outbox rows … COMMIT
  → 201  ◀── prospect is done here
  → background: attempt both sends, record outcome
```

**Marking a lead reached out**

```
PATCH /api/v1/leads/{id}  {"state": "REACHED_OUT"}
  → verify JWT, re-check is_active     401
  → load lead                          404
  → assert_can_transition()            409
  → set state, reached_out_at, reached_out_by
  → append lead_state_event
  → return the lead with its full audit trail
```

---

## 6. Failure modes

| Failure | Behaviour | Prospect sees |
|---|---|---|
| SMTP unreachable | Rows marked `FAILED` with the error; visible in the UI | `201` — nothing wrong |
| Object storage down | Upload fails before commit; no partial lead | `500`, safe to retry |
| Database down | Nothing commits; no orphaned storage object beyond a stray file | `500`, safe to retry |
| Process dies mid-dispatch | Rows stay `PENDING`; queryable and visible | `201` — already delivered |
| Malicious upload | Rejected at the byte level | `415` |
| Form spam | Sliding-window limiter | `429` with `retry_after_seconds` |
| Token expires mid-session | `apiFetch` catches the 401 | Redirected to login with a notice |

---

## 7. What I'd do next

Ordered by what I'd reach for first in production.

1. **Email retry worker.** The schema is ready. A loop selecting `status != 'SENT' AND attempts < 5 AND next_attempt_at <= now()` with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (so replicas don't double-send) and exponential backoff. Delivery becomes at-least-once; a duplicate confirmation beats a silent loss.
2. **Distributed rate limiting.** The current limiter is in-process — correct for one instance, useless across replicas and reset on deploy. Move to Redis or the edge.
3. **Virus scanning.** Magic-byte validation proves a file is a well-formed PDF, not that it is safe. A real deployment should scan resumes (ClamAV or a managed scanner) before an attorney downloads one.
4. **Token revocation.** Logout currently just drops the cookie; the JWT stays valid until expiry. Short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token, or a revocation list.
5. **Observability.** Logs are already structured JSON with request ids. Next: metrics on submission rate, delivery failure rate and transition latency, plus an alert on `FAILED` deliveries.
6. **Richer lead pipeline.** More states (`IN_REVIEW`, `QUALIFIED`, `REJECTED`), assignment to a specific attorney, and internal notes. The state machine and audit table were built to absorb this without restructuring.
7. **Idempotency on submission.** An `Idempotency-Key` header would let a client retry a timed-out POST without creating a duplicate lead.

---

## 8. Testing

68 tests. Integration tests run against **real Postgres**, not SQLite, so the
enum types, server defaults and cascade behaviour under test are the ones that
ship. Storage and email use in-memory fakes — the suite is fast, deterministic
and offline.

| File | Covers |
|---|---|
| `test_state_machine.py` | Legal and illegal transitions, 409 payloads |
| `test_upload_validation.py` | Spoofed extensions, zip-not-docx, size cap, content-beats-name |
| `test_rate_limit.py` | Budget, per-client isolation, window expiry |
| `test_auth.py` | Login, case-insensitivity, enumeration resistance, mid-session deactivation |
| `test_leads_public.py` | Intake, outbox atomicity, mail-failure isolation, validation |
| `test_leads_internal.py` | Access control, pagination, search, transitions, audit trail, download |

The tests worth reading first are
`test_email_failure_does_not_fail_the_submission` (the outbox guarantee),
`test_deactivation_invalidates_an_existing_token` (why `is_active` is checked
per-request), and `test_resume_is_stored_under_a_generated_key` (path traversal).

# API reference

Base URL: `http://localhost:8000` · All endpoints under `/api/v1` except health checks.
Interactive docs: **http://localhost:8000/docs**

## Error envelope

Every non-2xx response has the same shape, so a client needs exactly one parser:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "The submitted data is invalid.",
    "details": { "fields": { "email": "value is not a valid email address" } }
  }
}
```

`details.fields` is present on `422` and maps field name → message, so a form
can render each error under the right input.

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `validation_error` | 422 | Bad or missing fields |
| `unauthorized` | 401 | Missing, invalid or expired token |
| `account_inactive` | 401 | Account has been deactivated |
| `not_found` | 404 | No such resource |
| `invalid_state_transition` | 409 | Transition not legal from the current state |
| `payload_too_large` | 413 | Resume exceeds the cap |
| `unsupported_media_type` | 415 | Resume is not a PDF or DOCX |
| `rate_limited` | 429 | Too many submissions |
| `internal_error` | 500 | Unexpected — details are logged, never returned |

---

## Public

### `POST /api/v1/leads`

Submit a lead. **No authentication.** Rate limited per IP (default 10/min).

`Content-Type: multipart/form-data`

| Field | Type | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| `first_name` | string | required, 1–100, trimmed |
| `last_name` | string | required, 1–100, trimmed |
| `email` | string | required, valid address, lowercased |
| `resume` | file | required, PDF or DOCX **verified by magic bytes**, ≤ 5 MB |

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/leads \
  -F first_name=Ada -F last_name=Lovelace \
  -F email=ada@example.com -F resume=@cv.pdf
```

**`201 Created`**
```json
{ "id": "…", "state": "PENDING", "created_at": "2026-08-08T02:31:27Z" }
```

Nothing else is echoed back to an unauthenticated caller. Both emails are
enqueued in the same transaction and dispatched after the response — a mail
failure does not affect this status code.

---

## Auth

### `POST /api/v1/auth/login`

```json
{ "email": "attorney@example.com", "password": "changeme123" }
```

**`200`** → `{ "access_token": "…", "token_type": "bearer", "expires_in": 3600 }`

Email matching is case-insensitive. Unknown accounts and wrong passwords return
an identical `401` so the endpoint cannot be used to enumerate addresses.

### `GET /api/v1/auth/me`

Requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Returns the current attorney.
`is_active` is re-checked here and on every authenticated request, so
deactivation takes effect immediately rather than at token expiry.

---

## Internal

All require `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

### `GET /api/v1/leads`

| Query | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | 1 | |
| `page_size` | 20 | max 100 |
| `state` | — | `PENDING` \| `REACHED_OUT` |
| `q` | — | matches first name, last name, full name or email; `%` and `_` are literal |
| `sort_by` | `created_at` | `created_at`, `updated_at`, `last_name`, `email`, `state` |
| `order` | `desc` | `asc` \| `desc` |

```json
{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "…", "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace",
      "email": "ada@example.com", "state": "PENDING",
      "created_at": "…", "updated_at": "…",
      "reached_out_at": null, "reached_out_by": null
    }
  ],
  "total": 42, "page": 1, "page_size": 20, "total_pages": 3
}
```

### `GET /api/v1/leads/stats`

`{ "PENDING": 12, "REACHED_OUT": 30 }` — counts for the filter tabs, one query.

### `GET /api/v1/leads/{id}`

Everything in the list item, plus resume metadata, the full audit trail and
per-email delivery status:

```json
{
  "id": "…", "first_name": "Ada", "state": "REACHED_OUT",
  "resume_filename": "Ada_CV.pdf",
  "resume_content_type": "application/pdf",
  "resume_size_bytes": 84213,
  "reached_out_at": "…",
  "reached_out_by": { "id": "…", "full_name": "Alma Attorney", "email": "…" },
  "state_events": [
    { "from_state": null, "to_state": "PENDING", "actor": null, "created_at": "…" },
    { "from_state": "PENDING", "to_state": "REACHED_OUT",
      "actor": { "full_name": "Alma Attorney", "…": "…" }, "created_at": "…" }
  ],
  "email_deliveries": [
    { "kind": "PROSPECT_CONFIRMATION", "to_address": "ada@example.com",
      "status": "SENT", "attempts": 1, "last_error": null, "sent_at": "…" },
    { "kind": "ATTORNEY_NOTIFICATION", "to_address": "attorney@example.com",
      "status": "SENT", "attempts": 1, "last_error": null, "sent_at": "…" }
  ]
}
```

A `state_event` with `actor: null` was the prospect's own submission.

**`404`** if no such lead · **`422`** if the id is not a UUID.

### `PATCH /api/v1/leads/{id}`

```json
{ "state": "REACHED_OUT" }
```

Records `reached_out_at`, `reached_out_by`, and appends a `lead_state_event`.
Returns the full detail object.

Illegal transitions return **`409`**:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "invalid_state_transition",
    "message": "Cannot move a lead from REACHED_OUT to PENDING.",
    "details": {
      "current_state": "REACHED_OUT",
      "requested_state": "PENDING",
      "allowed_states": []
    }
  }
}
```

### `GET /api/v1/leads/{id}/resume`

- **S3/MinIO** → `302` to a presigned URL (5 min TTL) with the original filename in `Content-Disposition`. Bytes never pass through the API.
- **Local disk** → `200` streaming the file directly.

The browser cannot call this directly (an `<a href>` sends no `Authorization`
header); the dashboard links to `/api/leads/{id}/resume` on the Next.js side,
which attaches the token and forwards the redirect.

---

## Health

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET /healthz` | Liveness — process is up |
| `GET /readyz` | Readiness — database reachable; `503` if not |

content.text:
Done. The full application is built, running, and verified from a clean rebuild.

## What's there

**Backend** (FastAPI, ~35 modules) — strict `routes → services → repositories → models` layering, with object storage and email behind swappable ports.

**Frontend** (Next.js 15 App Router) — public `/apply` form with drag-and-drop upload and inline validation; auth-guarded `/admin` dashboard with search, state filter tabs, pagination, lead detail with audit trail and per-email delivery status.

**Infra** — one `make up` brings up Postgres, MinIO, MailHog, API and web.

## Verified on a from-scratch rebuild

I tore down all volumes and ran the documented quick start (`make up`, `make seed`), then walked the whole flow:

| | |
|---|---|
| Migrations apply to an empty DB | ✅ |
| Public submit → `201` | ✅ |
| Both emails in MailHog | ✅ prospect + attorney |
| Login → httpOnly cookie | ✅ |
| Dashboard renders the lead | ✅ |
| `PENDING → REACHED_OUT` w/ actor + 2 audit events | ✅ |
| Resume download via UI proxy, bytes match | ✅ |
| Detail page shows history + delivery status | ✅ |
| 68 tests · ruff · tsc · eslint | ✅ all clean |

## Worth knowing

**Eight real bugs surfaced during verification**, several design-level rather than typos — a startup crash from a union return type, `CORS_ORIGINS` being JSON-decoded before validation, `EmailStr` rejecting `.test` domains so the shipped seed account couldn't log in, `EmailStr` on *response* schemas (which would 500 on stored data), a stale identity map serialising a null attorney, and `middleware.ts` sitting at the project root where Next never loaded it — meaning `/admin` was completely unguarded until I moved it to `src/`.

**The outbox proved itself during development.** The background dispatcher raced the commit and found no lead. Nothing was lost: the lead and both delivery rows had committed atomically, and the two emails sat visible as `PENDING` rather than vanishing. That's the exact failure the design existed to survive, and it's now pinned by a test.

**Three limitations are documented rather than hidden** — no email retry (schema is ready; it's a pure addition), in-process rate limiting (single-instance only), and client-side logout (JWTs stay valid until expiry). All in the README and `docs/system-design.md` §7.

One environment note: **Postgres is on host port 5433**, since your `another-project-db` container owns 5432. It's configurable via `POSTGRES_HOST_PORT` and I left your other project untouched.

The stack is running now — http://localhost:3000/apply and http://localhost:3000/admin/leads (`attorney@example.com` / `changeme123`). `make clean` tears it down.

content.text:
It all worked — the email exists, addressed to you, with your actual resume filename. It just never left the machine.

**Why:** in the design phase we chose *"SMTP + MailHog, pluggable"*. MailHog is a fake SMTP server that swallows every message so local testing can't accidentally email real people. Open **http://localhost:8025** and you'll see both emails, with the HTML version rendered properly (the branded layout, not the plain text above).

## If you want it to actually reach your Gmail

It's a config change, not a code change — that's what the `EmailBackend` port is for. Edit `.env`:

```bash
SMTP_HOST=smtp.gmail.com
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USERNAME=harshini.venkataraman@gmail.com
SMTP_PASSWORD=<16-char Google App Password>
SMTP_USE_TLS=true
EMAIL_FROM=harshini.venkataraman@gmail.com
ATTORNEY_NOTIFICATION_EMAIL=harshini.venkataraman@gmail.com
```

Then `docker compose up -d --force-recreate backend` (a plain `restart` won't pick up new env — I hit that earlier).

Two caveats: Gmail needs an [App Password](https://myaccount.google.com/apppasswords) with 2FA on, since it rejects plain account passwords for SMTP. And `EMAIL_FROM` must match the authenticated account or Gmail will reject the send. For anything beyond a demo, a transactional provider (Resend, SendGrid, SES) is the better target — same three env vars.

Worth noting: if the credentials are wrong, the submission still returns `201` and the failure shows up as a `FAILED` row with the SMTP error on the lead's detail page, rather than breaking the form. That's the outbox doing its job — so you'd see exactly why it didn't send.

Want me to wire up real delivery? I'd need you to generate the App Password — I won't ask you to paste it here; you can put it straight into `.env` yourself and I'll recreate the container and test it.

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

That wasn't your typing — it was my bug. Sorry.

**What happened:** my `conftest.py` used `os.environ.setdefault("DATABASE_URL", ...)` to point the test suite at a throwaway `alma_test` database. But docker-compose already sets `DATABASE_URL` in the container, so `setdefault` did nothing. The suite ran against your real `alma` database, and its `TRUNCATE`-between-tests fixture deleted the seeded attorney account. The credentials were correct; the account simply no longer existed.

**Fixed two ways:**
1. Unconditional assignment, deriving `<name>_test` from whatever `DATABASE_URL` is set — so it can't silently no-op again.
2. A hard guard at collection time that refuses to run if the target database name doesn't end in `_test`. Verified: `alma` → REFUSED, `production` → REFUSED, `alma_test` → allowed.

**Proven fixed** — I seeded the dev database, ran the full suite, and re-counted:

```
users in dev DB before tests: 1
68 passed in 16.91s
users in dev DB after tests:  1
```

content.content: Launching skill: artifact-design

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.text:
Draw as the engineer who has to live with the decision, not as a decorator: a diagram earns its place when it lets a cold reader see a mechanism they would otherwise have to assemble from prose — where data flows, which components talk, what changes between two options, what state a request moves through. If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on — the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves — and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes — the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on — no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` — no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end — never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11–13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool — simplify instead.

Alma Leads · architecture

How the front end and back end actually talk

Four distinct channels connect Next.js to FastAPI, and which one a given interaction uses is a deliberate choice about where the auth token is allowed to exist. This walks each one, lists every API call, and gives the reasoning behind the decisions that shaped them.

  • The shape of the system
  • The four channels
  • Every API call
  • Flow: submitting a lead
  • Flow: signing in
  • Flow: marking reached out
  • Why these decisions

The shape of the system

Two populations use this application and they get very different treatment. A prospect is anonymous, arrives from the open internet, and touches exactly one endpoint. An attorney is authenticated, and every byte they see passes an auth check first.

That split is why there isn't one uniform way the front end calls the back end. The public form has no token to protect, so it can call the API directly from the browser. Everything in the dashboard does have a token to protect — so none of it is allowed to run in the browser at all.

The four channels

Here is the part that usually surprises people: the dashboard makes almost no fetch calls from the browser. Reads happen during server rendering, writes happen through server actions, and the one thing that must be a plain browser request — a file download — gets a dedicated proxy.

1 · Public form → API, straight from the browser

lead-form.tsx is a client component that fetches NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL directly. Two reasons: there is no token to hide, and the resume is a file — proxying it through Next would buffer several megabytes twice for no benefit. This is the only call that needs CORS, which is why the API allows exactly one origin.

2 · Dashboard reads → server components

/admin/leads is an async server component. It calls apiGet(), which reads the httpOnly cookie, attaches Authorization: Bearer …, and returns typed data — all before any HTML reaches the browser. The browser receives rendered markup and never sees the token or the API's address.

3 · Dashboard writes → server actions

Clicking Mark as reached out invokes updateLeadState(), a server action. It PATCHes the API and then calls revalidatePath(), so the list and detail views re-render from the database rather than from optimistic local state. If the API returns 409, the button surfaces that reason instead of silently disagreeing with the server.

4 · Resume download → route handler proxy

A plain <a href> cannot carry an Authorization header, so the link points at a Next route handler. It attaches the token, and — because storage is S3 — receives a 302 to a presigned URL which it forwards to the browser. The file bytes go straight from MinIO to the user and never traverse either server.

Consequence worth noticing

Because reads happen during server rendering, there is no loading spinner and no client-side data cache to invalidate. The trade is that every filter change is a navigation — which is why filter state lives in the URL rather than in React state, and why a filtered view is shareable.

Every API call

Ten endpoints. The Called from column is the important one — it tells you which of the four channels above carries each request.

Endpoint Called from Auth What it does
POST /api/v1/leads Browser, directly None Accepts the multipart form, validates the resume, writes the lead and its two outbox rows in one transaction.
POST /api/v1/auth/login Next route handler None Exchanges credentials for a JWT. The handler puts it in an httpOnly cookie so the browser never holds it.
GET /api/v1/auth/me Admin layout (server) Bearer Resolves the signed-in attorney for the header. Also re-checks is_active.
GET /api/v1/leads Leads page (server) Bearer Paginated list with state, q, sort_by, order.
GET /api/v1/leads/stats Leads page (server) Bearer Per-state counts for the filter tabs, in a single grouped query.
GET /api/v1/leads/{id} Detail page (server) Bearer Full lead plus its audit trail and per-email delivery status.
PATCH /api/v1/leads/{id} Server action Bearer Transitions state. Records the actor and appends an audit event. 409 if the move is illegal.
GET /api/v1/leads/{id}/resume Next route handler Bearer 302 to a 5-minute presigned URL, or streams the file when storage is local disk.
GET /healthz Orchestrator None Liveness — the process is up.
GET /readyz Orchestrator None Readiness — the database answers. 503 if not.

Every non-2xx response uses one envelope — { error: { code, message, details } } — so the front end has a single parser. On a 422, details.fields maps field name to message, which is exactly what the form needs to mark the right input.

Flow: submitting a lead

This is the flow with the most design in it, because it is the one where something outside our control — the mail provider — can fail while a member of the public is watching.

  1. The rate limiter checks the caller's IP, then field validation runs.
  2. The resume is streamed with a running byte counter and its magic bytes are checked. Failures here return 415 or 413 and nothing is written.
  3. The file goes to object storage before the transaction — an orphaned file is harmless; a lead row pointing at a missing resume is not.
  4. One transaction inserts the lead, its initial audit event, and two email_deliveries rows marked PENDING.
  5. Commit. The 201 returns here — the prospect is finished.
  6. A background task attempts both sends and writes back SENT or FAILED with the error.
This wasn't theoretical

During development the background task raced the commit and found no lead to send for. Nothing was lost: the lead and both delivery rows had committed atomically, and the two emails sat visible as PENDING instead of vanishing. The fix was to commit before scheduling dispatch — but the outbox is what turned a silent data-loss bug into a visible one.

Flow: signing in

The goal is that the token exists in exactly two places — the FastAPI process that signed it, and an httpOnly cookie no script can read.

middleware.ts guards /admin, but only by checking that a cookie is present. That is a user-experience measure, not security — a forged cookie sails straight past it and into a 401 from FastAPI, which verifies the signature and re-checks the account. Putting real enforcement in the middleware would mean two systems deciding who is allowed in, and eventually they would disagree.

Why the account is re-checked every request

A JWT stays cryptographically valid until it expires. If the API trusted the token's claims, a deactivated attorney would keep working for up to an hour. Instead is_active is read from the database on every authenticated call, so revocation takes effect on the next click.

Flow: marking reached out

The one mutation in the product, and the reason there is a state machine rather than an UPDATE.

The PATCH sets the state, stamps reached_out_at and reached_out_by, and appends a row to lead_state_events. That append-only table is why the detail page can show a history at all — without it, state is a single mutable cell and the answer to who marked this, and when is gone on the next write.

The response returns the whole lead including the refreshed audit trail, and the server action calls revalidatePath(). The UI never guesses what the new state is; it re-reads it.

Why these decisions

Each of these had a simpler option that was rejected for a specific reason.

A transactional outbox instead of sending email inline

Sending inline makes the prospect wait on your mail provider, and forces a bad choice when it fails: return 500 and invite a duplicate submission (the lead is already saved), or swallow the error and let the attorney never learn the lead exists. The second fails silently, which is worse. Moving the send to a background task fixes latency but not loss — the intent lives only in memory.

Cost
One extra table and about eighty lines.
Buys
Atomicity, plus observability — "which leads never got their notification" becomes a WHERE clause, and delivery status renders on the lead page.

Validating resumes by their bytes, not their filename

The accept attribute and the declared Content-Type are both set by the client, so neither is evidence. A PDF must begin %PDF-; a DOCX must be a zip whose directory actually contains word/. An executable renamed .pdf is rejected. Storage keys are generated server-side, never derived from the uploaded filename — that name is attacker-controlled, and using it invites path traversal.

Cost
Reading the zip directory; buffering to a spooled temp file.
Buys
The public upload endpoint stops being a way to put arbitrary content in your bucket under a name you trust.

Deactivating attorneys instead of deleting them

reached_out_by_id and the audit trail's actor_id are foreign keys into users. Deleting a departing attorney nulls those out and puts holes in the record exactly where accountability matters. is_active exists so that revoking access and destroying history are different operations.

Cost
One boolean column and one check in the auth path.
Buys
"Who marked this lead?" stays answerable after someone leaves.

httpOnly cookies instead of a token in JavaScript

Storing a JWT in localStorage is simpler and means any XSS bug anywhere on the origin hands over the session. Keeping it in an httpOnly cookie and reading it only on the server costs a route handler and means data fetching has to happen during rendering — which is precisely why the dashboard is built out of server components.

Cost
Filter state must live in the URL; no client-side cache.
Buys
The session is not reachable by script, and filtered views are shareable as a side effect.

Presigned URLs instead of streaming files through the API

Streaming means every resume download occupies an application worker for the duration of the transfer. A presigned URL is a 302 the API answers in milliseconds, after which the bytes move directly from object storage to the browser. The local-disk adapter cannot presign, so it streams — both paths exist and both are exercised.

Cost
A short-lived signed URL leaves your control for five minutes.
Buys
Downloads do not consume application capacity.

Ports for storage and email

These are the two dependencies the application does not own. Behind an interface, MinIO becomes S3 and MailHog becomes SendGrid by changing environment variables — and the test suite substitutes in-memory fakes, so it runs offline and deterministically.

Cost
An abstraction layer over two dependencies.
Buys
Swapping providers is configuration, and tests never touch the network.

What is deliberately not built

  • Email retry. A FAILED row stays failed. The columns attempts and next_attempt_at already exist, so the worker is an addition rather than a migration.
  • Distributed rate limiting. The current limiter counts in process memory — correct for one instance, useless across replicas.
  • Token revocation. Signing out drops the cookie; the JWT itself stays valid until it expires.
Source of truth lives in the repository — docs/system-design.md for the long form, docs/api.md for the endpoint reference, and the 68 tests under backend/tests/ for the behaviour these decisions are supposed to produce.

  1. The rate limiter checks the caller's IP, then field validation runs.
  2. The resume is streamed with a running byte counter and its magic bytes are checked. Failures here return 415 or 413 and nothing is written.
  3. The file goes to object storage before the transaction — an orphaned file is harmless; a lead row pointing at a missing resume is not.
  4. One transaction inserts the lead, its initial audit event, and two email_deliveries rows marked PENDING.
  5. Commit. The 201 returns here — the prospect is finished.
  6. A background task attempts both sends and writes back SENT or FAILED with the error.
This wasn't theoretical

During development the background task raced the commit and found no lead to send for. Nothing was lost: the lead and both delivery rows had committed atomically, and the two emails sat visible as PENDING instead of vanishing. The fix was to commit before scheduling dispatch — but the outbox is what turned a silent data-loss bug into a visible one.

Flow: signing in

The goal is that the token exists in exactly two places — the FastAPI process that signed it, and an httpOnly cookie no script can read.

middleware.ts guards /admin, but only by checking that a cookie is present. That is a user-experience measure, not security — a forged cookie sails straight past it and into a 401 from FastAPI, which verifies the signature and re-checks the account. Putting real enforcement in the middleware would mean two systems deciding who is allowed in, and eventually they would disagree.

Why the account is re-checked every request

A JWT stays cryptographically valid until it expires. If the API trusted the token's claims, a deactivated attorney would keep working for up to an hour. Instead is_active is read from the database on every authenticated call, so revocation takes effect on the next click.

Flow: marking reached out

The one mutation in the product, and the reason there is a state machine rather than an UPDATE.

The PATCH sets the state, stamps reached_out_at and reached_out_by, and appends a row to lead_state_events. That append-only table is why the detail page can show a history at all — without it, state is a single mutable cell and the answer to who marked this, and when is gone on the next write.

The response returns the whole lead including the refreshed audit trail, and the server action calls revalidatePath(). The UI never guesses what the new state is; it re-reads it.

Why these decisions

Each of these had a simpler option that was rejected for a specific reason.

A transactional outbox instead of sending email inline

Sending inline makes the prospect wait on your mail provider, and forces a bad choice when it fails: return 500 and invite a duplicate submission (the lead is already saved), or swallow the error and let the attorney never learn the lead exists. The second fails silently, which is worse. Moving the send to a background task fixes latency but not loss — the intent lives only in memory.

Cost
One extra table and about eighty lines.
Buys
Atomicity, plus observability — "which leads never got their notification" becomes a WHERE clause, and delivery status renders on the lead page.

Validating resumes by their bytes, not their filename

The accept attribute and the declared Content-Type are both set by the client, so neither is evidence. A PDF must begin %PDF-; a DOCX must be a zip whose directory actually contains word/. An executable renamed .pdf is rejected. Storage keys are generated server-side, never derived from the uploaded filename — that name is attacker-controlled, and using it invites path traversal.

Cost
Reading the zip directory; buffering to a spooled temp file.
Buys
The public upload endpoint stops being a way to put arbitrary content in your bucket under a name you trust.

Deactivating attorneys instead of deleting them

reached_out_by_id and the audit trail's actor_id are foreign keys into users. Deleting a departing attorney nulls those out and puts holes in the record exactly where accountability matters. is_active exists so that revoking access and destroying history are different operations.

Cost
One boolean column and one check in the auth path.
Buys
"Who marked this lead?" stays answerable after someone leaves.

httpOnly cookies instead of a token in JavaScript

Storing a JWT in localStorage is simpler and means any XSS bug anywhere on the origin hands over the session. Keeping it in an httpOnly cookie and reading it only on the server costs a route handler and means data fetching has to happen during rendering — which is precisely why the dashboard is built out of server components.

Cost
Filter state must live in the URL; no client-side cache.
Buys
The session is not reachable by script, and filtered views are shareable as a side effect.

Presigned URLs instead of streaming files through the API

Streaming means every resume download occupies an application worker for the duration of the transfer. A presigned URL is a 302 the API answers in milliseconds, after which the bytes move directly from object storage to the browser. The local-disk adapter cannot presign, so it streams — both paths exist and both are exercised.

Cost
A short-lived signed URL leaves your control for five minutes.
Buys
Downloads do not consume application capacity.

Ports for storage and email

These are the two dependencies the application does not own. Behind an interface, MinIO becomes S3 and MailHog becomes SendGrid by changing environment variables — and the test suite substitutes in-memory fakes, so it runs offline and deterministically.

Cost
An abstraction layer over two dependencies.
Buys
Swapping providers is configuration, and tests never touch the network.

What is deliberately not built

  • Email retry. A FAILED row stays failed. The columns attempts and next_attempt_at already exist, so the worker is an addition rather than a migration.
  • Distributed rate limiting. The current limiter counts in process memory — correct for one instance, useless across replicas.
  • Token revocation. Signing out drops the cookie; the JWT itself stays valid until it expires.
Source of truth lives in the repository — docs/system-design.md for the long form, docs/api.md for the endpoint reference, and the 68 tests under backend/tests/ for the behaviour these decisions are supposed to produce.
